title: Adobe MAX 2026 is all about AI agents, smarter editing, and fewer creative headaches
summary: Adobe MAX 2026 focuses on AI agents and smarter editing tools
detailed: Adobe announced major AI-powered upgrades across Firefly, Creative Cloud, and GenStudio at Adobe MAX 2026, centering on AI agents to automate creative workflows.
The new Adobe Creative Agent (in beta) powers features like a Plan Mode, Model Selector, and third-party model access from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, Kling, Topaz Labs, and ElevenLabs.

Desktop apps including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io are receiving integrated AI agent capabilities and tools such as Relight, Generative Restyle, and Color Mode.

Adobe previewed local Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations planned for early 2027 private beta to let third-party AI agents work natively on project files while keeping layers and vectors editable.
This release matters because it shifts Adobe's software from manual editing tools to automated, multi-step agentic workflows that span desktop apps, web ecosystems, and enterprise marketing.
sentences: Adobe wants creators to spend less time wrestling with software and more time actually creating.
At Adobe MAX 2026, the company has announced a major wave of AI-powered upgrades across Firefly, Creative Cloud, and GenStudio, with AI agents taking centre stage.
The announcements cover everything from generating videos and editing photos through natural language to automating repetitive creative tasks.
Adobe is also strengthening its partnerships with Google and Microsoft, bringing its tools into more of the apps people already use.
In short, Adobe wants to become the creative toolbox that does a little bit of everything, preferably before the coffee gets cold.
Firefly is arguably getting the biggest makeover.

Adobe is expanding it from an AI image and video generator into a more complete creative studio, bringing image editing, video production, design tools, third-party AI models, and its new Creative Agent together.
Users can access models from companies including Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, Kling, Topaz Labs, and ElevenLabs, giving them more choices without having to jump between different platforms.
The star of the show is the Adobe Creative Agent, which powers the Firefly AI Assistant in beta.
Instead of manually navigating several tools, creators can describe what they want and let the agent coordinate multiple steps.
New customization options let users save brand colours, formats, characters, and product preferences.
There's also a Plan Mode, where users can review and approve the agent's approach before it gets to work, and a Model Selector to choose which AI model handles a particular task.
Always-on agents are also in preview, allowing recurring jobs such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms to run in the background.
Firefly's individual creative tools are getting attention, too.
Firefly Video can turn a story idea into scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll.
Firefly Image adds tools such as Edit Object, Edit Text, Relight, and Retouch, allowing users to change specific parts of an image without disturbing everything else.
Quick Actions offers ready-made tasks such as removing objects or generating thumbnails, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, 3D, and print into one workspace.

Firefly Graph lets creators build reusable workflows, while Firefly Builder is being previewed as a way to turn natural-language descriptions into interactive prototypes of websites, presentations, and apps without writing code.
Professional creators aren't being left out of the AI party.
Adobe is extending its Creative Agent into desktop applications including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io.
In Premiere, the agent can apply effects across multiple clips, track masked subjects, and adjust colour and exposure across an entire sequence.
That's the kind of repetitive timeline work editors would happily hand over to an assistant.
Photoshop gets Relight, which lets users adjust lighting, and Generative Restyle, which turns prompt-based edits into adjustable controls.
There's also an improved Remove Tool, Quick Compare for checking before-and-after edits, and an AI-assisted editing experience.

Premiere gets Color Mode for more controlled colour grading, a Generative Media Tool for creating video, sound effects, soundscapes, and music directly in the timeline, plus tools to clean up dialogue and separate sound sources.
Generative Remove can also erase unwanted objects from footage.
Lightroom adds Glow, Blemish Removal, and an Open Eyes feature in beta, while InDesign introduces real-time Co-editing in beta and flexible layouts.
Illustrator gets refreshed content libraries and on-canvas Blend controls.
Adobe is also previewing local Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations for Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects.
These will allow third-party AI agents to work directly with native project files on a user's computer.
Importantly, layers, vectors, sequences, and other project elements remain editable, so creators can still make manual adjustments instead of being handed one flattened AI-generated result.
The integrations are planned for private beta in early 2027.
For businesses, Adobe is bringing its CX Enterprise Coworker into GenStudio to help marketing teams plan campaigns, create personalized content variations, and maintain brand consistency at scale.

Its Brand Intelligence system can adapt designs to different formats while keeping brand guidelines intact, and Workfront gets an AI-powered Ideation Space for turning campaign ideas and performance data into structured briefs.
The Google partnership will bring Acrobat into Google Drive and Gmail, expand Adobe's tools across Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode, and introduce Google's image and video models into Adobe apps.
Adobe and Google DeepMind are also exploring new AI-powered Photoshop editing capabilities.
Meanwhile, Microsoft is bringing optimized Photoshop, Premiere, After Effects, and Substance 3D Painter to high-performance Arm-based Windows PCs.
Adobe Express features are also coming to Microsoft Photos, letting users expand photos, remove objects, and access design templates without constantly switching apps.
Adobe might be a little late to the AI party, but it's certainly not showing up empty-handed.
DaVinci Resolve and Canva have already made impressive strides with AI-powered creative tools and MCP integrations, so Adobe isn't exactly reinventing the wheel here.
However, its real strength lies in bringing these capabilities into an ecosystem that millions of creators already rely on.
Having powerful AI agents work directly inside Photoshop, Premiere, and Illustrator, without disrupting familiar workflows, could be a much bigger deal than simply adding another flashy AI feature.
And that's where Adobe could have the upper hand.
Rather than asking professionals to switch platforms or learn entirely new tools, it's making the software they already know considerably smarter.
Whether that's enough to win back creators who've jumped ship to competing platforms remains to be seen, but for existing Creative Cloud users, these upgrades look genuinely promising.
Adobe may not have been first to the AI race, but with its massive creative ecosystem behind it, it has every chance of making a serious comeback.
